name: Human zoo
scope: The set of ideas the defining sources find behind the practice of exhibiting people, mostly colonised or non-European peoples, in zoos, fairs and colonial expositions from the 1870s to about 1958 (Hagenbeck's shows, the 1889 Paris 'Negro village', Tervuren 1897, St. Louis 1904, Brussels 1958): that peoples sort into a hierarchy of civilised and 'primitive', that Western rule is justified by it, and that such peoples are fit to be put on show. CNRS (Boëtsch, Blanchard) gives the racial hierarchy and colonial-racism reading; the Staged Otherness volume and Guardian give the 'ethnic show' and colonial-display accounts; Planet Wissen gives the German Völkerschauen aim of making Europeans look 'civilized'. Scholars contest how far 'human zoo' fits every show (Staged Otherness prefers 'ethnic shows'): this profile takes only what the sources say the displays stood for. It excludes later novelty displays (Adelaide 2007, London 2005) and today's critics' positions, which only show it is an ideology.

aliases.name: Ethnic shows
aliases.quote: Although the catchy term “human zoos” has been propagated by the French researcher Pascal Blanchard (e.g., Bancel et al. 2002), I strongly pre- fer the term “ethnic shows” (Völkerschauen in German).

keyFigures.role: German animal dealer who from 1874-75 staged the Völkerschauen that set the model for human zoos
keyFigures.quote: Im Jahr 1875 stellte der Hamburger Zoodirektor Carl Hagenbeck in seinem Tierpark eine Familie aus Lappland

summary: Human zoos (ethnic shows, Völkerschauen) were public exhibitions of non-European and colonised peoples in zoos, fairs and colonial expositions from the 1870s to the 1950s. The sources present them as staging a hierarchy of 'civilised' Europeans over 'primitive' peoples, tied to scientific racism and used to win public support for colonial rule as a civilising mission. Scholars dispute how far the label fits every show.

furtherReading.note: Short overview of the exhibitions, scientific racism and colonial politics.

furtherReading.note: Scholarly volume arguing 'ethnic shows' fits better than 'human zoos'.
